sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) combined with lenvatinib has demonstrated efficacy for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, real-world evidence on the additional benefit of PD-1 inhibitors in conversion therapy remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of triple therapy (TACE, lenvatinib, and PD-1 inhibitors) versus dual therapy (TACE and lenvatinib) in conversion therapy for initially unresectable HCC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This multicenter study was conducted in 20 Chinese tertiary hospitals. Patients received either triple therapy (TLP group, n = 289) or dual therapy (TL group, n = 132). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to control for confounding. Multivariate models compared overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: From January 2019 to June 2023, 421 consecutive patients were enrolled. After IPTW adjustment, baseline characteristics were well balanced. The TLP group showed superior efficacy: objective response rate 55.1% versus 34.7% (p < 0.001), complete response rate 24.9% versus 14.9% (p = 0.010), and conversion surgery rate 35.5% versus 15.7% (p < 0.001). Median OS was prolonged (31.67 vs. 25.00 months; adjusted HR 0.60, 95% CI: 0.42–0.85, p = 0.001) and median PFS extended (16.47 vs. 12.00 months; adjusted HR 0.65, 95% CI: 0.47–0.93, p = 0.008). Sensitivity analyses including propensity score matching (HR 0.61), landmark analysis (HR 0.64), and time-varying covariate analysis (HR 0.58) confirmed the findings. E-value analysis (2.72) suggested unmeasured confounding alone is unlikely to explain the benefit. Treatment effects were consistent across subgroups. Grade 3–4 adverse events were similar (35.6% vs. 36.4%, p = 0.885), though immune-related adverse events were more frequent in the TLP group.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Adding PD-1 inhibitors to TACE plus lenvatinib was associated with improved tumor response, prolonged survival, and higher conversion surgery rates, with an acceptable safety profile. Given the heterogeneity of PD-1 inhibitors and inherent limitations of retrospective design, these findings should be considered hypothesis generating and require verification in prospective randomized controlled trials.
Keywords: Hepatocellular carcinoma, Transarterial chemoembolization, Lenvatinib, PD-1 inhibitors, Inverse probability of treatment weighting

abstract.title: Plain Language Summary
abstract.p: Liver cancer is one of the deadliest cancers worldwide. When liver cancer cannot be removed by surgery, doctors use treatments to shrink tumors, so surgery may become possible later. This is called “conversion therapy.” We studied 421 patients from 20 hospitals in China whose liver cancer could not be surgically removed at first. One group received two treatments: TACE (a procedure that blocks blood flow to tumors while delivering chemotherapy directly to them) plus lenvatinib (a pill that stops tumor blood vessel growth). The other group received these same treatments plus a PD-1 inhibitor, which helps the body’s immune system fight cancer. The group receiving all three treatments had better results. More patients saw their tumors shrink (55% versus 35%), and more were able to have surgery to remove their cancer (35% versus 16%). Patients receiving the three-treatment combination also lived longer, about 32 months compared to 25 months. Side effects were similar between groups. The most common included tiredness, changes in liver function tests, and decreased appetite. These findings suggest that adding immune therapy may help more patients with advanced liver cancer live longer and have a better chance of curative surgery. However, this was not a randomized trial, so more research is needed to confirm these results.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common malignancy worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths [1]. Although curative surgical treatment can achieve long-term survival in early-stage disease, most patients are not candidates for surgical resection at diagnosis, with 5-year survival rates below 10% [2]. Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) is recommended as the standard treatment for intermediate-stage HCC according to current guidelines and is the most widely used treatment for advanced HCC in real-world practice [3, 4]. Recent evidence has demonstrated clear clinical benefits of TACE combined with systemic therapy. The EMERALD-1 trial showed that TACE plus durvalumab improved patient outcomes [5], while multiple real-world studies including CHANCE001, GUIDANCE001, and CHANCE2201 have confirmed that TACE combined with targeted therapy and immunotherapy significantly improves survival outcomes compared to TACE alone or systemic therapy alone [6–8]. In recent years, immunotherapy represented by immune checkpoint inhibitors has demonstrated potent antitumor activity. Following the positive results from landmark trials such as IMbrave150 and ORIENT-32, the combination of programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1) inhibitors with anti-angiogenic molecular targeted agents has emerged as a promising and guideline-recommended therapeutic strategy for HCC [9–11]. Lenvatinib is an oral small-molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor that selectively targets multiple pathways including vascular endothelial growth factor receptor, platelet-derived growth factor receptor, and fibroblast growth factor receptor. Based on the results of the REFLECT study, it has been established as a first-line treatment for unresectable HCC. It demonstrated superior objective response rates (ORRs) compared to sorafenib (24.1% vs. 9.2%) with similar overall survival (OS) [12].

The combination of TACE with anti-angiogenic and immunotherapy has a strong theoretical foundation. The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment of HCC is typically associated with poor prognosis [13, 14]. TACE can transform immunosuppressive “cold tumors” into “hot tumors” by inducing immunogenic tumor cell death and tumor-specific immune responses, releasing tumor antigens, pro-inflammatory cytokines, vascular endothelial growth factor, and hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, thereby providing potential synergistic antitumor effects in combination with anti-PD-1 and molecular targeted therapy [15, 16]. Simultaneously, TACE exacerbates tumor hypoxia, leading to hypoxia-inducible factor-1α accumulation, upregulation of PDGF and VEGF expression, promotion of angiogenesis-induced collateral vessel formation, and subsequent tumor vascular remodeling and local recurrence [17–19]. Therefore, anti-angiogenic agents such as lenvatinib can effectively counteract the vascular remodeling process following TACE.

Furthermore, studies have demonstrated synergistic effects between lenvatinib and immune checkpoint inhibitors [20, 21]. VEGF is a highly expressed angiogenic factor in the HCC tumor microenvironment that supports tumor growth and promotes immune escape, serving as a key mediator in the immunosuppressive microenvironment [22]. Lenvatinib can alleviate immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment by inhibiting VEGF and increase T-lymphocyte infiltration in immunosuppressive microenvironments, providing an effective immunotherapeutic microenvironment for immune checkpoint inhibitors to exert their effects [23].

For patients with initially unresectable HCC, conversion therapy has received increasing attention as an emerging therapeutic strategy. Conversion therapy aims to downsize or induce necrosis in initially unresectable tumors through effective multimodal treatment, thereby creating opportunities for curative resection and ultimately improving long-term survival [24, 25]. Notably, combining systemic therapy with locoregional treatment has emerged as a key strategy to facilitate such curative conversion in initially unresectable HCC [26]. Although the combination of TACE with lenvatinib has demonstrated good efficacy in multiple studies, complete response rates remain limited in the field of conversion therapy [27, 28]. Theoretically, adding PD-1 inhibitors to the combination of TACE and lenvatinib may produce synergistic effects, improving tumor response rates and conversion surgery success rates.

Several small-sample studies have preliminarily explored the triple therapy strategy combining TACE, lenvatinib, and PD-1 inhibitors, showing encouraging results [29, 30]. However, there is currently a lack of large-scale, multicenter comparative studies to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety advantages of this triple therapy. Additionally, most existing studies are single-center, small-sample exploratory investigations, with the majority not employing rigorous statistical methods to control for selection bias and confounding factors, limiting the reliability and generalizability of their results.

Based on this background, this study aims to systematically compare the efficacy and safety of triple therapy (TACE combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors) versus dual therapy (TACE combined with lenvatinib) in conversion therapy for initially unresectable HCC through a multicenter retrospective cohort study, employing inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) methods to control for confounding factors [31]. We hypothesize that triple therapy can significantly improve tumor response rates, prolong survival, increase conversion surgery opportunities, and maintain an acceptable safety profile, providing preliminary evidence-based medical evidence for clinical practice and establishing an important foundation for future prospective randomized controlled trials.

sec.title: Study Design and Participants
sec.p: This multicenter retrospective study included patients with initially unresectable HCC who received TACE combined with lenvatinib with or without PD-1 inhibitors (sintilimab [Innovent, China], tislelizumab [BeiGene, China], camrelizumab [Hengrui, China], or pembrolizumab [Merck, USA]) as conversion therapy between January 2019 and June 2023. The data for this study were extracted from the “Guangxi Liver Cancer Clinical Study Alliance (GUIDANCE)” registry, curated by the Liver Cancer Committee of the Guangxi Anticancer Association [7]. HCC diagnosis was established through pathological or clinical diagnosis based on the Chinese Guidelines for Primary Liver Cancer [32] and the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system [33]. Initially unresectable HCC was defined as tumors that could not achieve complete resection due to oncological or technical limitations, as assessed by a multidisciplinary team consisting of hepatobiliary surgeons, interventional radiologists, medical oncologists, and radiologists. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of all participating centers. The study was conducted in strict accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki of the World Medical Association. The study was reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines [34].

The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) patients with HCC confirmed by histology, cytology, or clinical diagnosis according to American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases or European Association for the Study of the Liver standards; (2) age ≥18 years and ≤75 years; (3) initially unresectable disease as determined by multidisciplinary team assessment; (4) Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage A, B, or C; (5) Child-Pugh liver function class A or B without uncontrolled ascites or hepatic encephalopathy; (6) Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status score 0–1; (7) adequate hematological and biochemical parameters (hemoglobin ≥90 g/L, absolute neutrophil count ≥1.5 × 109/L, platelet count ≥60 × 109/L, total bilirubin ≤3 times the upper limit of normal, alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase ≤5 times the upper limit of normal); (8) at least one measurable intrahepatic lesion ≥1 cm according to RECIST 1.1 criteria; (9) follow-up time ≥3 months. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age >75 years; (2) patients who had previously received systemic or local treatment for HCC; (3) ECOG performance status score ≥2 or Child-Pugh class C; (4) patients with other malignancies within 5 years; (5) severe cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases or dysfunction of other vital organs; (6) pregnant or lactating women; (7) patients who received treatment for less than one cycle, except for those who discontinued treatment due to intolerable adverse events; (8) patients with incomplete clinical or follow-up data.

sec.title: Treatment Allocation
sec.p: The TLP group was defined as receiving TACE within 60 days of PD-1 inhibitor initiation, with lenvatinib given concurrently with either TACE or PD-1 inhibitors, and at least one cycle of PD-1 inhibitor after TACE. Treatment decisions were made through shared decision-making between the MDT and patients following BCLC or Chinese National Liver Cancer guidelines. The choice between TLP and TL was influenced by: (1) drug availability and reimbursement status; (2) economic considerations; (3) patient preferences regarding immune-related adverse events; (4) physician experience with immunotherapy management. Treatment sequencing (TACE-first vs. systemic-first) and intervals between components were recorded. In clinical practice, treatment allocation was not based on predefined protocol criteria but on a pragmatic shared decision-making process. The principal drivers were (1) drug accessibility: PD-1 inhibitors were unavailable at some participating centers during the early study period (2019–2020) because NMPA approvals for HCC-specific indications were granted between 2018 and 2021 on a staggered timeline; (2) financial constraints: the addition of a PD-1 inhibitor increased per-course treatment costs by approximately JPY 50,000–100,000 (≈USD 7,000–14,000), and before inclusion in the National Reimbursement Drug List, many patients declined immunotherapy because of out-of-pocket burden; (3) patient concern about immune-related toxicity: some patients opted for the dual regimen after informed discussion, particularly those with pre-existing autoimmune conditions or strong aversion to potential immune-mediated organ injury; (4) physician experience: during the earlier study period, some treating physicians at smaller centers had limited experience managing immune-related adverse events and were more conservative in recommending triple therapy. We acknowledge that these pragmatic factors do not constitute objective, protocol-driven allocation criteria, and this is an inherent limitation of the retrospective real-world design. Baseline data collected included demographics, etiology, AFP, ECOG, Child-Pugh class, BCLC stage, cirrhosis status, tumor characteristics, macrovascular invasion, extrahepatic metastasis, and laboratory parameters.

sec.title: TACE Procedures
sec.p: TACE was performed by experienced interventional radiologists (≥10 years experience) following standardized protocols [32]. Patients received conventional TACE (cTACE) or drug-eluting bead TACE per institutional practice. For cTACE, chemotherapy drugs (doxorubicin 20–60 mg, epirubicin 30–75 mg, or oxaliplatin 100–150 mg/m2) were mixed with iodized oil (5–20 mL) and injected followed by gelatin sponge embolization. drug-eluting bead TACE used drug-eluting beads (DC Bead, 100–300 μm) pre-loaded with chemotherapy. TACE technique distribution and chemotherapy agents were recorded. TACE strategy was individualized based on tumor burden: selective/super-selective catheterization for oligonodular disease (≤3 lesions) targeting all tumor-feeding arteries; staged treatment for multinodular disease (>3 lesions) prioritizing dominant lesions. For patients with portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT), TACE was performed only if technically feasible with super-selective catheterization, reduced embolic dose, and confirmed adequate collateral circulation. Patients with complete main portal vein occlusion without collaterals were excluded from TACE. Subsequent TACE was performed on-demand based on imaging assessment. The number of TACE sessions was recorded. TACE was discontinued for Child-Pugh C deterioration, ECOG >2, or continuous progression after three consecutive treatments.

sec.title: Systemic Therapy
sec.p: Lenvatinib was administered orally (12 mg daily for ≥60 kg, 8 mg for <60 kg), with dose reduction permitted for toxicity. PD-1 inhibitors (sintilimab, tislelizumab, camrelizumab, or pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks) were selected based on availability, cost, and physician preference. PD-1 inhibitor distribution was recorded. For Child-Pugh B patients, reduced initial lenvatinib doses were used. Dose modifications were recorded for both groups. The TL group received TACE plus lenvatinib without PD-1 inhibitors. Treatment was discontinued for progression, unacceptable toxicity, or patient/physician decision.

sec.title: Follow-Up and Assessments
sec.p: Follow-up duration was calculated using reverse Kaplan-Meier method. Data cutoff was December 31, 2024. Imaging (CT/MRI) was performed every 6–8 weeks. Tumor response was assessed by two independent radiologists per mRECIST and RECIST 1.1 [35]. Safety assessment was conducted according to National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 (NCI-CTCAE v5.0), with evaluations every 2–4 weeks during treatment, including physical examinations, laboratory tests, and symptom assessments [36]. The feasibility of conversion surgery was evaluated by a multidisciplinary team consisting of hepatobiliary surgeons, interventional radiologists, medical oncologists, and radiologists. Conversion success was defined as patients deemed suitable for curative resection by multidisciplinary team assessment. Long-term follow-up was conducted every 3 months until patient death. Conversion surgery criteria were standardized across centers based on Chinese HCC conversion therapy guidelines: (1) Technical criteria: adequate future liver remnant (≥30% normal, ≥40% cirrhotic), feasible R0 resection; (2) oncological criteria: tumor response without new lesions, AFP decline >50% if elevated; (3) functional criteria: Child-Pugh A or early B (≤7), ECOG 0–1, no decompensation; (4) timing criteria: ≥4 weeks from systemic therapy, ≥4–6 weeks from TACE, adverse events ≤grade 1.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint was OS, defined as time from first treatment component initiation to death or last follow-up. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), ORR, disease control rate (DCR), conversion surgery rate, and safety. To avoid immortal time bias, OS and PFS were calculated from first treatment initiation, not PD-1 inhibitor start. The 60-day window accommodated clinical practice patterns of sequential treatment initiation. For conversion surgery patients, PFS assessment continued postoperatively; R0 resection patients were progression free until documented recurrence.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), and categorical variables were expressed as frequency (percentage). Comparisons of continuous variables between groups were performed using independent samples t test or Mann-Whitney U test, and categorical variables were compared using χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test. To reduce the impact of selection bias and confounding factors, IPTW method was employed [37]. Propensity scores were estimated via logistic regression including age, gender, etiology, cirrhosis, ECOG, Child-Pugh, BCLC stage, AFP, tumor number/size, macrovascular invasion, extrahepatic metastasis, bilirubin, and albumin. Balance was assessed by standardized mean difference (<0.1 indicating good balance). The analysis hierarchy was prespecified: the primary analysis was IPTW-adjusted Cox proportional hazards regression for OS and PFS. All other analyses, including propensity score matching (PSM), landmark analysis, time-varying covariate analysis, E-value analysis, leave-one-out analysis, and subgroup analyses, were considered sensitivity or exploratory analyses intended to assess the robustness of primary findings rather than to draw independent conclusions. Sensitivity analyses included (1) PSM (1:1, caliper 0.2); (2) landmark analysis at 60 days; (3) time-varying covariate analysis treating PD-1 exposure as time varying; (4) E-value analysis for unmeasured confounding [38]; (5) leave-one-out analysis excluding each PD-1 inhibitor type. Survival was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test. Cox regression calculated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CI. Subgroup analyses were presented via forest plots. All analyses used R version 4.3.0, with two-sided p < 0.05 considered significant.

sec.title: Patient Characteristics
sec.p: Between January 2019 and June 2023, we screened 2,382 patients with initially unresectable HCC from 20 major medical centers in China. After applying eligibility criteria, 421 patients were finally included for analysis, of whom 289 received TLP treatment (TACE combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors) and 132 received TL treatment (TACE combined with lenvatinib) (shown in Fig. 1). Baseline characteristics were balanced before IPTW (all p > 0.05): median age 58–59 years, male predominance (84.1–87.1%), hepatitis B etiology (78.8–80.3%), cirrhosis (81.3–84.8%) (Table 1). After IPTW, all standardized mean differences were <0.1, achieving excellent balance (shown in Fig. 2). The weighted cohort included 265 TLP and 121 TL patients. Median follow-up was 24.5 months (IQR: 16.2–32.8), 25.2 months (17.1–33.5) for TLP and 23.1 months (14.8–31.2) for TL. Minimum follow-up for survivors was 12 months.

sec.p: TACE-first strategy was used in 73.7% (213/289) of TLP and 74.2% (98/132) of TL patients. (p = 0.912). Median interval to complete therapy initiation was 7 days (IQR: 0–21) for TLP; 78.2% received all components within 14 days, 91.0% within 30 days (online suppl. Table S1; for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000552409). cTACE was used in 83.4% vs. 81.8% (p = 0.672). Chemotherapy agents included epirubicin (64.7% vs. 66.7%), doxorubicin (21.6% vs 19.4%), and pirarubicin (13.7% vs 13.9%), with no significant differences (online suppl. Table S2). Among 160 patients (38.0%) with macrovascular invasion, 112 (26.6%) had PVTT: Vp1/Vp2 69.6%, Vp3 24.1%, Vp4 6.3%. Median TACE sessions were 2 (IQR: 1–3) vs. 2 (1–4) (p = 0.156). More TL patients required ≥4 sessions (18.2% vs. 10.7%, p = 0.035). PD-1 inhibitor distribution was as follows: sintilimab 43.9%, tislelizumab 26.3%, camrelizumab 20.1%, pembrolizumab 9.7% (online suppl. Table S3). Among 55 Child-Pugh B patients (13.1%), 78.2% received reduced initial lenvatinib doses. Dose reduction occurred in 33.9% vs 31.1%, interruption in 23.2% vs. 21.2% and discontinuation in 8.0% vs. 6.8%. Among the 7 patients with Vp4 PVTT (main portal vein or contralateral branch involvement per Cheng’s classification), all were treated at high-volume tertiary centers by interventional radiologists with >15 years of experience. In all 7 cases, TACE was performed only after the following prerequisites were confirmed: (1) the presence of well-developed hepatopetal collateral circulation (cavernous transformation or arterial compensation) documented on pre-procedural CT angiography or mesenteric angiography; (2) preserved hepatic function (Child-Pugh A in 6 patients, Child-Pugh B7 in 1 patient); (3) technical feasibility of super-selective catheterization to target tumor-feeding arteries while minimizing non-target embolization; (4) multidisciplinary team consensus that the potential benefit outweighed the risk. None of the 7 patients had complete main portal vein occlusion without collateral circulation. All procedures were performed using sub-segmental super-selective technique with reduced embolic agent doses (lipiodol ≤5 mL per session). No procedure-related mortality or hepatic decompensation occurred in this subgroup. Detailed clinical characteristics are provided in online supplementary Table S4.

sec.title: Therapeutic Efficacy
sec.p: By mRECIST, TLP achieved superior ORR: 55.0% vs 34.8% (p < 0.001), with higher CR (24.9% vs 15.2%, p = 0.024) and PR (30.1% vs. 19.7%, p = 0.026). DCR was similar (72.0% vs. 69.7%, p = 0.636). By RECIST 1.1, ORR was 33.2% vs. 20.5% (p = 0.008) and DCR 72.3% vs. 60.6% (p = 0.017). After IPTW, differences remained significant: mRECIST ORR 55.1% vs. 34.7% (p < 0.001); RECIST 1.1 ORR 33.2% vs. 20.7% (p = 0.005), DCR 72.5% vs 61.2% (p = 0.010) (Table 2). Conversion surgery was achieved in 123 patients (29.2%): 35.3% (102/289) vs. 15.9% (21/132) (p < 0.001); after IPTW: 35.5% vs. 15.7% (p < 0.001). Surgical patients had superior survival: median OS not reached vs. 22.3 months (HR = 3.42, p < 0.001), 2-year OS 78.5% vs. 41.2%. Within TLP, surgical patients achieved 2-year OS 80.2% vs. 48.6% for non-surgical. Median RFS was 18.5 vs. 14.2 months (p = 0.156) (online suppl. Table S5). Among the 123 patients who underwent conversion surgery, 112 (91.1%) achieved R0 resection (TLP: 93/102, 91.2%; TL: 19/21, 90.5%; p = 0.916). Recurrence-free survival analysis restricted to R0 resection patients (n = 112) showed TLP group (n = 93): median RFS 19.2 months (95% CI: 15.8–24.1), 1-year RFS 67.7%, 2-year RFS 44.1%; TL group (n = 19): median RFS 15.6 months (95% CI: 9.2–22.5), 1-year RFS 52.6%, 2-year RFS 31.6% (HR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.37–1.39, p = 0.198) (online suppl. Fig. S1). While a numerically favorable trend was observed for TLP patients, the difference did not reach statistical significance, reflecting the limited sample size in the TL surgical subgroup.

sec.title: Safety Analysis
sec.p: Safety profiles were similar. Common adverse events included fatigue (28.4–30.3%), elevated transaminases (27.3–30.3%), and decreased appetite (27.3–29.5%). Grade 3–4 adverse events were comparable (35.6% vs. 36.4%, p = 0.885). TLP showed increased thyroid dysfunction (11.4% vs. 7.6%, p = 0.005) and grade 3–4 hyperbilirubinemia (10.0% vs. 2.3%, p = 0.005) (Table 3). In TLP, any-grade irAEs occurred in 42.9% (124/289), grade 3–4 in 9.7% (28/289). Common irAEs included skin reactions 18.0%, thyroid dysfunction 14.2%, hepatotoxicity 8.0%, pneumonitis 5.2%. Corticosteroids were required in 54.0%; PD-1 discontinuation in 14.5%. Two treatment-related deaths occurred (pneumonitis, myocarditis) (online suppl. Tables S6, S7).

sec.title: Survival Analysis
sec.p: Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated that the TLP group achieved significantly superior survival outcomes compared to the TL group. For OS, the TLP group showed a median OS of 31.63 months versus 25.00 months in the TL group (HR = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.41–0.82, p = 0.002), representing a 42% reduction in death risk, with death event rates of 35.3% (102/289) versus 47.7% (61/132) during follow-up (shown in Fig. 3a). Similarly, PFS was significantly prolonged in the TLP group, with a median PFS of 16.47 months versus 12.00 months (HR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.48–0.94, p = 0.010), representing a 33% reduction in progression risk (shown in Fig. 3b). The survival curves showed early separation between the two groups, suggesting early benefit from TLP treatment. After IPTW adjustment, these survival benefits were further confirmed, with adjusted median OS of 31.67 months versus 25.00 months (HR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.42–0.85, p = 0.001) and median PFS remaining at 16.47 months versus 12.00 months (HR = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.47–0.93, p = 0.008) (shown in Fig. 4).

sec.p: Multiple sensitivity analyses confirmed the findings; leave-one-out analyses showed consistent benefit, excluding sintilimab (HR = 0.58); tislelizumab (HR = 0.62); camrelizumab (HR = 0.59); pembrolizumab (HR = 0.61). Heterogeneity was nonsignificant (I2 = 0%) (online suppl. Table S8). First, PSM using 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching with a caliper of 0.2 yielded 118 matched pairs. In the matched cohort, the survival benefit of TLP remained significant: median OS was 31.70 months versus 25.00 months (HR = 0.61, 95% CI: 0.41–0.91, p = 0.018), and median PFS was 21.40 months versus 12.00 months (HR = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.35–0.79, p = 0.002) (online suppl. Fig. S2); second, landmark analysis at 60 days from treatment initiation included 273 patients in the TLP group and 119 patients in the TL group who remained alive and event free at the landmark. The survival benefit of triple therapy was confirmed: median OS from landmark was 31.63 months versus 25.00 months (HR = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.44–0.91, p = 0.014), and median PFS from landmark was 16.00 months versus 12.00 months (HR = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.41–0.81, p = 0.002) (online suppl. Fig. S3); third, time-varying covariate analysis treating PD-1 inhibitor exposure as a time-varying covariate yielded a HR of 0.58 (95% CI: 0.41–0.83, p = 0.003) for OS and 0.64 (95% CI: 0.46–0.89, p = 0.008) for PFS (online suppl. Table S9).

To assess the robustness of our findings to potential unmeasured confounding, we calculated the E-value for the observed HR. The E-value for the OS benefit (HR = 0.60) was 2.72, with a lower confidence interval E-value of 1.63. This indicates that unmeasured confounding would need to be associated with both treatment selection and mortality by a risk ratio of at least 2.72-fold each, above and beyond the measured confounders, to fully explain away the observed treatment effect. This threshold exceeds the association strength of most known prognostic factors in HCC (e.g., ECOG status typically HR 1.5–2.5, Child-Pugh class HR 1.5–2.0, AFP level HR 1.3–1.8), suggesting that unmeasured confounding alone is unlikely to account for the observed survival benefit (online suppl. Tables S10, S11).

To assess whether the inclusion of Vp4 PVTT patients influenced the overall findings, we performed a sensitivity analysis excluding all 7 Vp4 patients (n = 414). The results were essentially unchanged: OS HR = 0.60 (95% CI: 0.42–0.86, p = 0.005) and PFS HR = 0.65 (95% CI: 0.46–0.92, p = 0.015) (online suppl. Table S12). To partially address the treatment sequence heterogeneity, we performed a restricted analysis limited to patients who initiated all treatment components within 7 days (near-simultaneous initiation). This subgroup included 171 TLP patients (59.2%) and 79 TL patients (59.8%). The survival benefit remained consistent: OS HR = 0.57 (95% CI: 0.37–0.88, p = 0.011) and PFS HR = 0.61 (95% CI: 0.41–0.91, p = 0.016) (online suppl. Table S13). To address the concern that conversion surgery is a post-baseline intermediate event that may mediate the treatment-survival relationship, we performed an additional Cox regression analysis incorporating conversion surgery as a time-dependent covariate. In this model, the HR for TLP vs. TL was 0.66 (95% CI: 0.46–0.95, p = 0.024) for OS, indicating that the survival advantage of triple therapy is not entirely explained by higher conversion surgery rates (online suppl. Table S14).

sec.title: Prognostic Factor Analysis
sec.p: Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified independent prognostic factors for OS. Poor prognostic factors included ECOG score 1 (HR = 2.19, 95% CI: 1.45–3.30, p < 0.001), Child-Pugh class B (HR = 1.63, 95% CI: 1.08–2.46, p = 0.021), tumor number > 3 (HR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.18–2.63, p = 0.006), maximum tumor diameter >5 cm (HR = 1.59, 95% CI: 1.05–2.41, p = 0.028), extrahepatic metastasis (HR = 1.87, 95% CI: 1.24–2.81, p = 0.003), and BCLC stage C (HR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.01–2.86, p = 0.046). Importantly, treatment regimen was an independent prognostic factor, with TL treatment significantly increasing death risk compared to TLP treatment (HR = 1.65, 95% CI: 1.11–2.46, p = 0.014) (Table 4).

sec.title: Subgroup Analyses
sec.p: Forest plot analysis showed that TLP treatment demonstrated consistent survival benefits in almost all predefined subgroups. For PFS, TLP treatment showed particularly significant benefits in multiple high-risk subgroups, including patients aged >60 years (HR = 1.81, p = 0.023), female patients (HR = 2.88, p = 0.016), Child-Pugh class B (HR = 1.91, p = 0.012), and AFP >400 ng/mL (HR = 1.91, p = 0.003) (shown in Fig. 5). Subgroup analysis results for OS were consistent with PFS, with beneficial trends observed for TLP treatment in all subgroups, with HRs all >1.0, indicating that TLP treatment can continuously reduce death risk, and the benefit is not affected by patient baseline characteristics (shown in Fig.6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This multicenter retrospective study compared triple therapy (TACE + lenvatinib + PD-1 inhibitors) versus dual therapy (TACE + lenvatinib) for conversion therapy in initially unresectable HCC. Our design directly addresses whether adding PD-1 inhibitors to TACE-lenvatinib provides additional benefit [12, 27, 28]. Results demonstrate significantly improved tumor response, prolonged survival, and acceptable safety with triple therapy.

Our study results demonstrated the unique value of immunotherapy in combination treatment for HCC. TLP achieved ORR 55.0% versus 34.8% (p < 0.001) by mRECIST, with CR 24.9% versus 15.2%. This substantial improvement in complete response predicts higher conversion success and better prognosis [39, 40], suggesting immunotherapy is a key component rather than merely supplementary.

The liver’s unique immune microenvironment provides theoretical foundation for these benefits [41, 42]. PD-1 inhibitors can reactivate suppressed T-cell function by blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway, restoring the body’s immune surveillance against tumors [43]. In our triple therapy strategy, TACE-induced immunogenic cell death releases tumor antigens, providing “fuel” for the immune system [44]; lenvatinib improves the tumor microenvironment through vascular normalization, enhancing immune cell infiltration; however, PD-1 inhibitors release the immune suppression “brake,” creating a perfect synergistic effect among the three components. This mechanistic complementarity explains why the addition of immunotherapy can produce such significant efficacy improvements [45]. In the current field of systemic treatment for unresectable liver cancer, anti-angiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors combined with or without immune checkpoint inhibitors have become guideline-recommended first-line treatment regimens. As highlighted in a recent review published by our research group, although multiple large randomized controlled trials have demonstrated the efficacy of these combination regimens, efficacy, safety, and drug pricing are the three most critical factors influencing clinical decision-making, and due to the lack of head-to-head comparative studies, clinicians still face challenges in treatment selection in actual practice [46], compared to major trials (IMbrave150, ORIENT-32, LEAP-002) showing ORR 10.8–29.8%, PFS 2.1–8.2 months, and OS 15.4–22.1 months for systemic therapy [10, 47, 48]. In contrast, the efficacy data from the TLP group in our study (ORR 55.0%, PFS 16.47 months, OS 31.67 months) demonstrated significant advantages of TACE combined with systemic treatment, further supporting the clinical value of local treatment combined with systemic treatment strategies.

The benefits of immunotherapy demonstrated durability characteristics in our study. Median OS extended from 25.00 months to 31.67 months, an extension of 6.67 months, representing a considerable magnitude of survival benefit in HCC treatment. More importantly, through Kaplan-Meier survival curves, it can be observed that the survival curves of the two groups separated early in treatment and this difference was maintained or even expanded over time, which is a typical manifestation of the long-term benefits of immunotherapy. Unlike traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy or molecular targeted therapy, once immunotherapy activates the body’s anti-tumor immune response, it can often produce durable immune memory, which may be an important reason for the long-term survival benefits achieved by triple therapy [49]. Subgroup analysis revealed consistent benefits across virtually all subgroups including high-risk patients (AFP >400, tumor >5 cm, Child-Pugh B) [50, 51]. This pattern of consistent benefits across subgroups emphasizes the unique advantages of immunotherapy as a systemic treatment modality, capable of activating systemic anti-tumor immune responses rather than being limited to local treatment effects.

From a safety perspective, our study confirmed the acceptability of immunotherapy. Although the TLP group showed increased incidence of specific immune-related adverse events such as thyroid dysfunction and hyperbilirubinemia, the overall incidence of grade 3–4 adverse events showed no significant difference compared to the TL group (35.6% vs. 36.4%, p = 0.885). This finding has important clinical significance, indicating that the toxicity of immunotherapy is controllable and manageable and does not bring unacceptable safety risks due to increased treatment intensity [52]. More importantly, immune-related adverse events are often markers of immune system activation and may, to some extent, predict better treatment outcomes [53].

Conversion surgery rate was 35.3% versus 15.9%, more than doubling curative treatment opportunities, substantially exceeding historical controls of TACE alone (10–20%) [54, 55], and TACE-sorafenib(28.8%) [56], and the extremely low complete response rates in early molecular targeted therapy [3]. Immunotherapy achieves deep responses through direct tumor killing and immune memory establishment [6, 57].

Our results align with GUIDANCE001 [7]. This multicenter study included 802 patients with initially unresectable liver cancer, comparing the efficacy of triple therapy combining TACE with various tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors versus TACE alone, showing that the triple therapy group had significantly superior OS compared to the TACE alone group (HR 0.43, 95% CI: 0.35–0.53), PFS of 15.9 months vs. 8.0 months, and higher conversion surgery rates (36.4% vs. 23.5%). Notably, the GUIDANCE001 study employed a combination strategy of various tyrosine kinase inhibitors (including lenvatinib, donafenib, apatinib, etc.) and different immune checkpoint inhibitors, while this study specifically focused on the specific standardized triple combination of TACE combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors. The high similarity of HR values between the two studies (0.58 vs. 0.43) and consistent survival benefit patterns not only mutually validate the reliability of study results but more importantly confirm that immunotherapy has universal value in liver cancer conversion therapy, regardless of the specific drug combination regimen employed.

We acknowledge that TACE in the setting of Vp4 PVTT is considered a relative or absolute contraindication by international guidelines such as EASL and AASLD. In our cohort, the decision to perform TACE in 7 patients with Vp4 involvement was made on a case-by-case basis at experienced high-volume centers, with strict prerequisites including confirmed collateral circulation and super-selective technique. This practice reflects Chinese national guidelines, which permit TACE for selected PVTT patients with demonstrated collateral flow and adequate liver reserve. Sensitivity analysis excluding all Vp4 patients confirmed that their inclusion did not drive the observed treatment effect (OS HR = 0.60, p = 0.005). We recognize that this approach may not be generalizable to all clinical settings, particularly centers with less interventional radiology expertise.

However, we must also recognize that the benefits of immunotherapy vary among individuals, and not all patients can derive the same degree of benefit. Biomarker-guided patient selection remains important, including PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite instability [58]. Optimal timing, dosing, and sequencing require further investigation [59, 60].

This study has several important limitations that must be acknowledged. First, treatment allocation was driven by pragmatic real-world factors – drug availability, cost, patient preference, and physician experience – rather than by predefined clinical criteria. Although statistical methods (IPTW, PSM, E-value analysis) were applied to adjust for measured confounders, these methods assume a well-defined, homogeneous intervention, which is only approximately satisfied in our setting where the TLP arm included four different PD-1 inhibitors and treatment decisions varied across institutions. These methods cannot address confounding arising from the allocation process itself or heterogeneity in treatment exposure, and our findings therefore represent associations observed under real-world conditions rather than established causal effects. Second, the absence of a standardized treatment backbone is a key limitation. Both groups included TACE-first (approximately 74%) and systemic therapy-first (approximately 26%) strategies with variable intervals between treatment components, making it difficult to attribute the observed differences solely to the addition of PD-1 inhibitors. Regarding monotherapy reference data, our previously published GUIDANCE001 study (Yang et al. Hepatology 2025) provided a TACE-alone control arm (n = 459), demonstrating that triple therapy significantly improved outcomes over TACE alone (OS HR = 0.43). However, within the current study, neither TACE-alone nor lenvatinib-alone arms are available, and GUIDANCE001 used heterogeneous TKIs rather than lenvatinib specifically. Therefore, the isolated incremental contribution of PD-1 inhibitors beyond the TACE + lenvatinib backbone cannot be precisely quantified from either study independently. Third, although participating centers agreed on common conversion surgery eligibility criteria derived from Chinese HCC conversion therapy guidelines, the final decision to proceed with surgery was made by each institution’s MDT and inevitably reflected local surgical expertise, risk tolerance, and case volume. We cannot exclude that inter-institutional variation in the threshold for recommending surgery contributed to the observed conversion rate differences. Conversion surgery represents a post-baseline intermediate event on the causal pathway between treatment and survival; our time-dependent covariate analysis showed an attenuated but persistent benefit (HR = 0.66), suggesting both direct and surgery-mediated treatment effects, though formal mediation analysis is beyond the scope of this retrospective study. Fourth, TACE in the setting of Vp4 PVTT is considered a relative or absolute contraindication by international guidelines such as EASL and AASLD; the inclusion of 7 such patients, treated at experienced high-volume centers with strict prerequisites, reflects Chinese clinical practice but may limit external validity. Finally, the study was not powered to detect differences between individual PD-1 inhibitors, and subtle agent-specific efficacy differences cannot be excluded. Prospective randomized trials with protocol-defined allocation, standardized treatment sequences, and appropriate control arms are essential to confirm these findings.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this multicenter real-world study, adding PD-1 inhibitors to TACE plus lenvatinib was associated with improved tumor response, higher conversion surgery rates, and prolonged survival in patients with initially unresectable HCC, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings are consistent with the survival benefit of TACE-based triple therapy observed in our GUIDANCE001 study and support the clinical value of immunotherapy within multimodal conversion strategies. However, given the heterogeneity of PD-1 inhibitors used, the non-randomized treatment allocation, and the inherent limitations of retrospective observational design, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis generating rather than confirmatory. Verification of this hypothesis will require prospective randomized controlled trials with protocol-defined treatment sequences, standardized regimens, and appropriate control arms.
